Apple Springs coupon rig — parameter explorer

This is a simulation of our planned bench experiment to test the effect of material and photoperiod on wastewater treatment. The simulation is designed to test various parameters to set the experiment in the optimal way. The physical experiment measures: (1) Ammonia levels. Top each vessel up and measure the ammonia concentration. Leave it, and measure it again 12 hours later — whatever is missing is what the biofilm consumed. Continue measuring and topping up throughout the experiment. (2) Biofilm (as coupon wet and dry rates) at days 3, 7, 10 and 28. This will tell us how much biofilm is there to do the work.

Predictions from an uncalibrated model — no coupon has been harvested yet. Every run is 28 days at a fixed 20 °C: temperature is an assumption here, not a measurement, and the bench rig needs a logger in each vessel to check it.

Move these controls to see how the rig geometry and the feeding schedule change what the experiment could measure.

0 = closed batch, the rig as originally configured.
Replacing the whole volume also carries away cells that have not attached yet.
The three destructive harvests, in days. Biomass is read off the simulated curve, so any day from 0.5 to 28 works. Day 28 is the end of the run and is always reported alongside them. reset to 3, 7, 10
Display only. The lamps run on a timer, so the daylength is set by the photoperiod above and does not depend on the calendar — changing this re-labels the axes and the harvest days, nothing else. clear

Biofilm on the coupon

Dashed lines mark the planned harvests at days 3, 7 and 10.

Nitrogen in the vessel liquid

Bench scale: the liquid around the coupons, not plant effluent, and not compared with the discharge permit. Watching ammonia fall and nitrate rise between refills is the primary measurement of the planned bench experiment — the gap between the concentration you topped up to and the one you read before the next refill, divided by coupon area and elapsed time, is the areal nitrification rate that carries over to the plant's discs. Nitrate climbing by roughly as much as ammonia falls is the check that the nitrogen was oxidized rather than simply taken up as cell material.

ammonia-N nitrate-N 2 mg/L — below this the nitrifiers are nitrogen-limited

What a day-10 harvest would contain

This panel stays at day 10 whatever the harvest days above are set to: the stored grid keeps the three-way split only at day 10, while the biomass curve is kept for the whole run. The three functional groups, and only one of them does the job the permit cares about. Nitrifiers are the organisms that turn ammonia into nitrate, so the rate measured in the panel above is essentially their biomass multiplied by how fast each cell works. Heterotrophs compete with them for surface and oxygen — more BOD in the feed means a thicker heterotrophic layer and less room for nitrifiers — while phototrophs neither help nor hinder directly, but add oxygen by day and take up some ammonia as cell material. A starved vessel yields almost pure algae, which is why it cannot constrain the competition or nitrification parameters.

phototrophs — use light nitrifiers — oxidise ammonia heterotrophs — consume BOD

pending input Functional-group fractions from published datasets. Every run starts from an assumed mix of 50 % phototrophs, 20 % nitrifiers and 30 % heterotrophs, and uses that same split for every cell that attaches over the 28 days. Nothing sources those numbers. An analysis of published rotating-biological-contactor metagenomes is planned to replace them with a sourced range, and, where the datasets record organic loading, to give a first bound on K_comp — the parameter this model is most sensitive to, and one the rig cannot measure as designed.

Planned measurements

What the bench experiment will actually record, and what each one pins down in the model above.

Once, before the run

Coupon wetted area and vessel working volume, once before the run — both are placeholders today, and together they set the coupon-area control on the left.

Surface roughness of each coupon material, once before the run — profilometry. Material enters the model only through an attachment factor taken from the literature, and roughness is the property most likely to separate the graphene coating from bare steel.

Contact angle on each coupon material, once before the run — sessile drop: a few µL of water photographed from the side. It measures wettability, which drives early attachment. Read it alongside the roughness, because roughness amplifies the angle you measure.

The liquid, twice a day

Ammonia-N and nitrate-N in the liquid, immediately before every refill — twice a day, about fifty paired readings over the run. Colorimetric kit and spectrophotometer, or an ammonia ion-selective electrode. Record the refill concentration and the clock time with each reading.

pH and alkalinity, on the same sample as the ammonia reading — pH meter and a simple titration. If the medium runs short of alkalinity buffer the vessel acidifies, nitrification slows below about pH 6.5, and the smaller ammonia drop can look like a poor material or photoperiod.

Solids in the discarded medium, filtered and weighed — that liquid is already being thrown away twice a day. It gives the detachment rate k_det directly, which nothing else in the rig measures.

Temperature in the liquid, logged continuously — one probe per vessel position. The model holds 20 °C fixed, but nitrification is strongly temperature-dependent.

The coupon, at each harvest

Coupon wet and dry weight, days 3, 7, 10 and 28. Lift the coupon, rinse off loose cells, dry at 105 °C and weigh; subtract the coupon's own clean mass, so every coupon must be weighed and labeled before it goes in. Destructive — each harvest consumes its coupon. A photograph at each harvest gives percent surface coverage from ImageJ, which is the model's colonized-fraction term.

Chlorophyll-a by solvent extraction at every harvest gives the phototroph share cheaply. Separating nitrifiers from heterotrophs needs sequencing, so that is planned for days 10 and 28 only; relative abundance multiplied by the dry weight above gives each group's areal biomass.

The Part 2 rig at day 10, rendered from the Blender model: three chambers, one per photoperiod, each holding four substrates × three replicates. Drag left or right to turn it. Vessel and coupon dimensions come from rig.yaml, so this is the same 25 cm² coupon in 1 L of liquor that the explorer is simulating.

drag to turn
liquor pale — ammonia spent liquor green — ammonia present deeper green — freshly fed

Color is a nutrient scale, not a permit check: these are bench vessels and the Outfall 001 limits do not apply to them. The lamp panel above each chamber is a reconstruction — no lamp, PAR or irradiance figure exists in any project document — and under the geometry modeled here the four substrate columns receive the same light to within 1 % — there is no substrate confound. The gradient runs along the replicate axis instead: the front and back rows sit about 20 % brighter than the middle one and are lit 13:1 from one face, while the middle row is lit evenly from both. Replicates are therefore not exchangeable, which is the case for measuring the field and randomizing vessel positions.

The coupon-scale biofilm model

A description of what the model is and how it works. Terms are defined in GLOSSARY.md; parameter values live in params_v2.yaml and rig dimensions in rig.yaml.

1. What it models

A single carrier coupon hanging in a stirred, illuminated vessel of synthetic wastewater. Three groups of organisms grow as a film on the coupon surface — phototrophs (algae and cyanobacteria, which need light), nitrifiers (which oxidize ammonia to nitrate and need oxygen), and heterotrophs (which eat dissolved organic matter and also need oxygen) — plus a fourth pool of cells still floating in the liquid. Cells land on the coupon from the liquid, grow, die, and slough off; while they do, they draw ammonia, nitrate, phosphorus and organic matter out of the liquid, which is replaced on a feeding schedule. The model tracks all of that through time and reports how much biomass sits on the coupon, how it is divided between the three groups, and how fast ammonia disappears.

The purpose is to compare carrier materials and geometries: which surface holds the most living, light-reached, oxygen-reached film per unit of reactor volume and per kilogram of carrier. The same equations run at two scales — one coupon in a beaker (the bench rig) and a packed carrier in a reactor (the screening study) — differing only in how much surface there is per unit volume.

2. State variables

Everything on the carrier is carried as areal biomass: grams of dry weight per square meter of carrier surface. Liquid concentrations are per cubic meter (numerically the same as mg/L).

Symbol Meaning Units
Snh ammonia-N in the liquid g N m⁻³
Sno nitrate-N in the liquid g N m⁻³
Sp soluble phosphorus in the liquid g P m⁻³
Sb biodegradable organic matter in the liquid g BOD m⁻³
Xpl suspended cells not yet attached g DW m⁻² of carrier
Xp phototrophs in the film g DW m⁻²
Xn nitrifiers in the film g DW m⁻²
Xh heterotrophs in the film g DW m⁻²

The three film groups are each resolved into irradiance bins — patches of the carrier that receive different amounts of light because of self-shading by the carrier itself. A bin b carries an area weight w_b (the fraction of carrier surface in that bin) and a relative irradiance E_b. The suspended pool is held in areal units too, so that every state is the same order of magnitude and the solver behaves.

3. The equations

3.1 Light reaching the cells

Light is attenuated twice: once by the carrier's own shape, once by the film.

I_b = I₀ · E_b                                   (carrier self-shading)
τ   = k_abs · Xp
Ī_b = I_b · (1 − e^(−τ)) / τ                     (Beer–Lambert through the film)

each patch of carrier starts with a fraction E_b of the incident light because neighboring surfaces shade it; the cells in that patch then shade each other, so the average cell sees less than the cells at the surface. The second line is the depth-average of exponential decay.

3.2 Phototroph growth

μ_p = μ_max,p · [Ī/(K_I+Ī)] · [N/(K_N,p+N)] · [Sp/(K_P,p+Sp)] · θ_p^(T−20) · free · α

growth runs at its maximum rate only when light, nitrogen (ammonia plus nitrate) and phosphorus are all plentiful; each shortage multiplies the rate down by a saturating (Monod) factor. Temperature scales it by the usual Arrhenius-style factor. free and α are defined below. Phototrophs grow only while the lamps are on, and respire at rate b_p only while they are off.

3.3 Carrying capacity — the film cannot grow forever

free = max(0, 1 − (Xp+Xn+Xh) / X_cap)

as the film thickens, less room is left; when the total areal biomass reaches X_cap all growth and all attachment stop. This is a single shared ceiling: a surface crowded with heterotrophs leaves no space for nitrifiers. Capacity is deliberately the same for every material — nothing has been measured that would justify giving the fabric a larger one — which is why the model predicts no lasting material difference except for graphene.

3.4 Nitrification

r_N = r_N,ref · (Xn/Xn,ref) · [Snh/(K_N,n+Snh)] · θ_n^(T−20) · f_comp · f_wet · [S_O/(K_O,A+S_O)] · free · α
f_comp = K_comp / (K_comp + Xh)

ammonia removal is proportional to how many nitrifiers are present, limited by how much ammonia there is and how much oxygen, and suppressed by heterotrophs — f_comp is the competition term: the more heterotrophs on the surface, the less of it nitrifiers hold. Nitrifier biomass then grows at yield Y_n per gram of nitrogen oxidized.

3.5 Heterotrophs are confined to the depth that BOD reaches

J_S   = Xh · μ_max,h / Y_h · [Sb/(K_S,h+Sb)]      (demand)
δ_S   = √(2 · D_S,eff · Sb / (J_S / L_f))         (penetration depth)
cap_h = ρ_dry · min(δ_S, L_f + δ_floor)
free_h = max(0, 1 − Xh/cap_h)

organic matter diffusing in from the liquid is consumed as it goes, so it only penetrates a certain depth. Heterotrophs can occupy only that depth; the rest of the film is left to the others. More BOD in the feed means a deeper heterotrophic layer and less room for nitrifiers, so the competition between the two is a consequence of diffusion rather than an imposed rule. The floor δ_floor (50 µm) lets a bare carrier be colonized at all.

3.6 Oxygen effectiveness

J_O2 = 4.57·r_N + (O₂ per BOD)·growth_h/Y_h − Y_O2,p·(photosynthesis − respiration)
δ    = √(2 · D_O2,eff · S_O / (J_O2 / L_f))
η    = min(1, δ / L_f)

add up how much oxygen the film demands, subtract what the phototrophs make, and ask how far oxygen can diffuse in before it is used up. If that depth is less than the film thickness, only that fraction of the film is aerobic, and the aerobic rates (nitrification and heterotrophic growth) are multiplied by η. Bulk dissolved oxygen S_O is imposed, not simulated — the vessel is stirred and open.

3.7 Attachment and detachment

j = k_att · a_mat · [Xpl/(K_pl+Xpl)]
d(Xp,Xn,Xh)/dt ← + j·fᵢ·free … − k_det·Xᵢ
dXpl/dt = Σ_b w_b (detached − attached) − b_pl·Xpl

cells land on the coupon at a rate set by how many are in suspension and how sticky the material is; the material factor a_mat is the only place material identity enters (apart from graphene, below). They leave again at a constant fractional rate. Attached and suspended cells are the same biomass moving between two places — nothing is created — and the pool runs down as it is drawn on, which is why a material advantage in attachment fades once the pool is depleted. Attachment is shut off by the same free term as growth, so it cannot push the film past capacity.

3.8 Lag

α(t) = 1 / (1 + (e^(ν·lag) − 1) · e^(−ν·t)),   ν = μ_max,h

real cells take hours to days to start growing after being transferred. This is the standard Baranyi–Roberts form: growth ramps from near zero up to full rate over about lag_d days. The model can express a lag; it currently does not — lag_d = 0, which makes α ≡ 1 exactly. The term is there so that the day 3 / 7 / 10 harvests can rule a lag in or out against a model capable of showing one. It delays growth only, not attachment.

3.9 Graphene

X_cap(t) = X_cap · [1 − (1 − 0.56)·(1 − e^(−(t−14)/10))]   for t > 14 d

A graphene-coated surface is modeled as bare steel with a capacity that falls as the film matures, reaching 56 % of the normal ceiling, after Romeu et al. (2022), who report 44 % less biofilm by wet weight at seven weeks with no effect during early attachment. Until coupon contact angle and roughness are measured this is the only difference between graphene and steel.

This is the model's weakest transfer, and it carries the whole graphene result. Romeu et al. tested graphene nanoplatelets dispersed in an epoxy resin, against glass and plain epoxy controls, in a marine system with marine cyanobacteria. The arm modeled here is a coating on stainless steel, compared against bare stainless steel, in wastewater. The authors further report that the dominant measured difference between composite and control was roughness, about 1000× higher — so the 44 % reduction may be a topographic effect of that composite rather than a property of graphene that a coating would reproduce. They also report larger reductions on other measures at seven weeks (54 % thickness, 82 % biovolume, 64 % surface coverage); wet weight is the smallest of the four and therefore the most conservative choice, but it is a choice. Because material differences otherwise wash out within about a week — attachment and detachment only change how fast a carrier reaches the same capacity-limited plateau — this single borrowed parameter is the only reason graphene behaves differently from steel at all. It should be replaced by a measurement on the project's own coupon before any graphene claim is made.

4. Area per unit volume (a_v)

Every rate in §3 is per square meter of carrier surface. What the experiment actually measures is a concentration in the liquid, and a_v (m² m⁻³) — wetted carrier area per unit of liquid volume — is what converts between the two:

r_v = a_v · Σ_b w_b · f_col,b · (1 − f_occ,b) · r_a,b

where w_b is the area fraction of irradiance bin b, f_col = 1 − e^(−X/2) is the colonized fraction of the surface, and f_occ is the share of pores bridged shut by the film. For a flat coupon the sum has few bins and no occlusion, and it reduces to a_eff · J_A, the form used in the manuscript.

For the bench rig a_v is one coupon's wetted area divided by the vessel's working volume, both from rig.yaml: currently 25 cm² in 1.0 L, giving a_v = 2.5 m² m⁻³. Both numbers are flagged provenance: placeholder and are waiting to be measured. a_v is the single number that sets how fast bulk concentrations move — the same film empties a small vessel quickly and a large one slowly — which is why it is the first control in the explorer, and why the feeding schedule has to be re-derived if the measurement comes back near 15 (three coupons, both faces) or 30 m² m⁻³. At 30 no manual schedule keeps up and the rig would need a pump.

f_occ is exploratory: it is computed and reported, but the headline ranking is given with and without it, because nothing has been measured against which to check it.

Out of scope for this round. The same equation extends to a packed carrier in a reactor, where a_v, the pore-aperture distribution and the irradiance bin weights are built by geometry.py and irradiance.py from a voxelized carrier. That pipeline exists and drives the carrier screening study, but nothing in the bench experiment tests it, so reactor-scale extrapolation is deliberately left for later.

5. Parameters

Status: L from the literature or the plant model · D derived or calibrated from such a value · U unmeasured, given a defensible value and varied in the ensemble. No parameter is yet measured on this system; that is what the bench experiment is for. Author–year keys resolve in §8.

Which parameters matter

A Morris screening (8 trajectories × 15 parameters) ranks the elementary effects on the day-60 volumetric ammonia removal rate r_v (the response sensitivity.py actually ranks on; a second ranking on a_eff is computed alongside it):

K_comp 4373 ≫ rN_ref 1454 > D_O2_eff 802 > f_wet 754 > X_cap 716
> k_att 683 > S_O_bulk 544 > k_det 362 > b_p 184 > K_I 92 > I0 53

The two most influential parameters, K_comp and rN_ref, are both unmeasured. This is the model's largest weakness and the main thing the bench experiment should fix. It also drove a design change: in a closed batch the feed is exhausted within days and the film becomes ~90 % phototrophs, under which neither parameter can be constrained at all. The rig is therefore fed — half the volume replaced twice a day from day 3 — which keeps ammonia from falling below about 74 % of the nitrifier saturation level and keeps a nitrifying population to measure.

6. What the model does not include

  • Denitrification. Deliberately excluded; the rig is aerobic and nitrate accumulates.
  • pH and alkalinity. Not tracked, so alkalinity limitation of nitrification cannot appear.
  • Oxygen as a liquid state. Bulk DO is imposed; only its gradient inside the film is resolved.
  • Spatial structure within the film. Each irradiance bin is a stirred layer with analytic penetration depths, not a 1-D multi-species film model.
  • Inter-vessel variation. Every replicate in an arm is given the same light field, so the model cannot reproduce replicate scatter. The rig's lamp gradient runs along the replicate axis, not the material axis, and is not yet represented.
  • Specular reflection, inter-reflection, wavelength. The light model is diffuse and gray, so its irradiance estimates are a lower bound.
  • Nitrite as a separate species, and nitrate inhibition at high concentrations.
  • Temperature dynamics. Runs are isothermal at 20 °C; θ terms exist but are never exercised.
  • Any calibration to a measured growth curve. Nothing in the model has been fitted to data from these coupons.

7. Running it

python model/run_demo.py        # one arm, prints a summary and a figure
python model/build_explorer.py  # the parameter grid behind the web explorer
python model/build_page.py      # rebuild index.html from that grid and this file

Minimal use from Python:

import yaml, pandas as pd, reactor as R
par  = yaml.safe_load(open("params_v2.yaml"))["parameters"]
bins = pd.read_csv("irradiance_bins.csv").query("material=='FAB' and geometry=='Flat sheet'")
r = R.Reactor(par, bins.area_fraction.values, bins.rel_irradiance.values,
              a_v=2.5, attach=14.73, bulk_mode="batch",
              feed={"Snh": 30, "Sno": 0, "Sp": 5, "Sb": 50})
t, y = r.simulate(days=28, light_h=9.2, T=20.0)
u = r.unpack(y)                          # dict of Snh, Sno, Sp, Sb, Xp, Xn, Xh

Reactor(...) takes the parameter dict, the bin weights and relative irradiances, the specific area a_v, the material attachment factor, a bulk mode ("batch" for a closed vessel, "fixed" to hold the liquid constant) and the feed composition. simulate returns times and the raw state array; unpack turns it into named series and areal_rate returns the areal removal rate.

Requires Python 3.11+, numpy, scipy, pandas, pyyaml and matplotlib; rebuilding the page additionally needs markdown. Run from the repository root. The carrier geometry and irradiance pipelines referred to in §4 are not part of this release; their outputs ship as model/geometry_catalogue.csv and model/irradiance_bins.csv.

8. References

Every author–year key in §3 and §5 resolves here, with a note on what the model takes from each source. Several values reach the model second-hand: the entries drawn from Wolf et al. (2007) Table VI are that paper's own compilation, in places from Henze et al. (2000) and Eppley et al. (1969). Those compilations are cited as read, not as if the primary papers had been consulted.

Peer-reviewed literature

  • Baranyi, József; Roberts, Terry A. (1994). A dynamic approach to predicting bacterial growth in food. International Journal of Food Microbiology 23(3–4), 277–294. doi:10.1016/0168-1605(94)90157-0
    Used for: the Baranyi–Roberts lag form α(t) in §3.8. The form is implemented; lag_d = 0, so no lag is currently asserted.
  • Boelee, N.C.; Temmink, H.; Janssen, M.; Buisman, C.J.N.; Wijffels, R.H. (2011). Nitrogen and phosphorus removal from municipal wastewater effluent using microalgal biofilms. Water Research 45(18), 5925–5933. doi:10.1016/j.watres.2011.08.044
    Used for: phototroph biomass nitrogen and phosphorus content, fN_p = 0.048 and fP_p = 0.0099 g g⁻¹ DW, measured on a nutrient-replete microalgal biofilm.
  • Edmundson, Scott J.; Huesemann, Michael H. (2015). The dark side of algae cultivation: Characterizing night biomass loss in three photosynthetic algae, Chlorella sorokiniana, Nannochloropsis salina and Picochlorum sp.. Algal Research 12, 470–476. doi:10.1016/j.algal.2015.10.012
    Used for: the phototroph dark-decay rate b_p = 0.17 d⁻¹, from measured night biomass loss across three strains.
  • Gross, Martin; Zhao, Xuefei; Mascarenhas, Vernon; Wen, Zhiyou (2016). Effects of the surface physico-chemical properties and the surface textures on the initial colonization and the attached growth in algal biofilm. Biotechnology for Biofuels 9(1), 38. doi:10.1186/s13068-016-0451-z
    Used for: the material colonization factors a_mat (§3.7), taken as seven-day areal biomass relative to HDPE; the seven-day endpoint that mu_max_p is calibrated against; and the assay irradiance that stands in for I0 until this rig's lamp is characterized.
  • Ma, Shiyan; Huang, Yun; Zhang, Beiyu; Zhu, Xianqing; Xia, Ao; Zhu, Xun; Liao, Qiang (2023). Comprehensive modeling and predicting light transmission in microalgal biofilm. Journal of Environmental Management 326, 116757. doi:10.1016/j.jenvman.2022.116757
    Used for: the film light-absorption coefficient k_abs = 0.21 m² g⁻¹ DW (reported range 0.18–0.29), the Beer–Lambert term in §3.1.
  • Németh, András; Ainsworth, Jude; Ravishankar, Harish; Lens, Piet N. L.; Heffernan, Barry (2023). Temperature dependence of nitrification in a membrane-aerated biofilm reactor. Frontiers in Microbiology 14, 1114647. doi:10.3389/fmicb.2023.1114647
    Used for: the reference areal nitrification rate rN_ref = 4.2 g N m⁻² d⁻¹ (midpoint of 2.96–5.45 at 10–20 mg N L⁻¹) and the biofilm Arrhenius coefficient theta_n = 1.025. Measured in a membrane-aerated biofilm reactor, not an RBC — the transfer is why rN_ref is listed as unmeasured.
  • Romeu, Maria J.; Gomes, Luciana C.; Sousa-Cardoso, Francisca; Morais, João; Vasconcelos, Vítor; Whitehead, Kathryn A.; Pereira, Manuel F. R.; Soares, Olívia S. G. P.; Mergulhão, Filipe J. (2022). How do Graphene Composite Surfaces Affect the Development and Structure of Marine Cyanobacterial Biofilms?. Coatings 12(11), 1775. doi:10.3390/coatings12111775
    Used for: the graphene maturation factor in §3.9: 44 % less biofilm by wet weight at seven weeks, with no effect during early attachment. §3.9 sets out at length why this transfer is the model's weakest.
  • Wolf, Gundula; Picioreanu, Cristian; van Loosdrecht, Mark C.M. (2007). Kinetic modeling of phototrophic biofilms: The PHOBIA model. Biotechnology and Bioengineering 97(5), 1064–1079. doi:10.1002/bit.21306
    Used for: the PHOBIA parameter set, Table VI: K_N_p, K_N_n, K_S_h, Y_n, Y_h, b_n, b_h, and the nitrifier μ_max used to derive Xn_ref.

Books and model standards

  • Antonie, R. L. (2018). Fixed Biological Surfaces — Wastewater Treatment: The Rotating Biological Contactor. CRC Press. ISBN 9781351088947. Used for: the synthetic feed composition in rig.yaml — typical RBC effluent at BOD₅ 20, TSS 30, NH₃-N 20 mg L⁻¹. Cited second-hand, through the experiment setup document; the book itself has not been consulted here.

  • Henze, M., Gujer, W., Mino, T. & van Loosdrecht, M. C. M. (2000). Activated Sludge Models ASM1, ASM2, ASM2d and ASM3. IWA Scientific and Technical Report No. 9, IWA Publishing, London. Used for: the conventional suspended-growth Arrhenius coefficient 1.07 carried by theta_p and theta_h, and the decay rates that reach the model through Wolf et al. (2007).

Project documents (not peer-reviewed)

  • Copp, J. (2024). Modelling the Apple Springs Wastewater Treatment Plant. Technical Memorandum 136-002, Primodal Inc., 11 July 2024. Used for: the plant-model values the coupon model inherits — mu_max_h at 20 °C, the oxygen half-saturations K_O_A and K_O_H, the effective diffusivities D_O2_eff and D_S_eff, and the film density and moisture rho_film_wet = 1.426 g cm⁻³ and moisture = 0.85. The last two are assumptions in that model, not measurements — replacing them with a measured value is one of the things this experiment is for.
